subject: UserGWAS results changing depending on the number of SNPs - negative variances warning

messages.author: e5dd40a627510441
messages.subject: UserGWAS results changing depending on the number of SNPs - negative variances warning
parts:
Hi all, 

I'm running a UserGWAS (6 traits - 2 factors). When running the model without SNPs I ran into some high loadings close to/over 1. I was able to fix that with a model constraint for two indicators, solving the issue of negative variances. However, this problem came back when running the model with SNPS. I have ~6 million SNPs, so I split the SNP list into six (~1 million SNPs each). However, one of these files, more specifically 345 SNPs, returned a warning about some estimated ov variances being negative.

I decided to run the model again, but now only with these 345 SNPs. I was surprised to see that it ran without any errors or warnings. The estimates and p-values for those SNPs also changed. I also tried re-running other small sets of SNPs to make sure I was running the exact same model, and these showed the same estimates and p-values as before. So, this brings me to two questions:

1. If each SNP is independent of each other, how is it possible that the warnings only show up when running them together with other SNPs?

2. Again, considering that each SNP is independent, would it be okay then to ignore the estimates with the warnings and just consider the new ones that ran without warnings?


Here is the piece of code I used:

load(file="LDSCoutput_6.RData")

model = 'F1 =~ SSEEK + RISK + EXTR
F2 =~ PURG + BIS + PREMED
F1~~F2
F1 ~ SNP
F2 ~ SNP
SSEEK ~~ a*SSEEK
a > .001
PREMED ~~ b*PREMED
b > .001'

gwas = userGWAS(covstruc = LDSCoutput, SNPs = sumstats, model = model, std.lv = T, sub=c("F1~SNP", "F2~SNP"), parallel = T, cores = 15)

Best,
Dener

messages.author: d6d83e22ef3ba9f1
messages.subject: Re: UserGWAS results changing depending on the number of SNPs - negative variances warning
parts:
Hi Dener, 

Thanks for reaching out about this. My best guess as to why you are seeing different results for these SNPs depending on whether you use a full set of SNPs or just the 345 is because the first SNP run is used to produce starting values for all subsequent SNPs. This helps ease model convergence and speed-up run times when running as many models as there are SNPs in your dataset. 

Generally speaking, I do not expect which SNP is first to affect results in any meaningful way. This is why you reassuringly see the same estimates when running in small batches for the SNPs that did not produce warnings. This is with the exception that SNPs that produce more unstable model results (e.g., with the negative residual variances you are seeing for these 345) may be more likely to converge on different, presumably local, solutions depending on the start values. 

So to summarize, it sounds like if you let the model choose start values based on one of these 345 SNPs that it allows the model to converge on a more sensible solution as compared to start values from the other SNPs. Running these 345 SNPs on their own and using those estimates I would say is a reasonable troubleshooting strategy here. However, if these 345 SNPs do not produce significant effects on your two factors I might just drop them as it seems like they are more generally producing unstable estimates. 

If they are producing significant effects on the factors, I would suggest two additional sanity checks to make sure these are credible results. First, I would confirm that this isn't a sharp deviation from the data going in by confirming that the Z-statistics for the factor indicators are relatively large in the sumstats output. Second, I would suggest setting the smooth_check argument to TRUE and try rerunning these 345 again to confirm that these aren't SNPs that require a high degree of smoothing of the genetic covariance matrix (I generally recommend removing SNPs with Zs in this smooth_check column > 1.96). 

Best, 
  Andrew
